newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan says Sao Tome embassy set up amid China anger.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says Sao Tome embassy set up amid China anger.

text.p: Taiwan said on Saturday it has formally set up an embassy in the tiny African state of Sao Tome and Principe, sealing official relations between the two over fierce objections by Taiwan's rival, China.
Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government said it would not ask Sao Tome to sever ties with the communist government in China.
"The Republic of China's embassy in the Republic of Sao Tome and Principle has been formally established and has begun operation," Taiwan's foreign ministry said in a statement.
"As long as it does not affect or damage the friendship between us and Sao Tome, we will not demand that Sao Tome initiate a breakup with communist China," the ministry said.
Sao Tome President Miguel Trovoada confirmed earlier in May the establishment of relations with Taiwan, overruling an earlier parliament decision to oppose such a move.

Officials in Sao Tome, one of the world's poorest states, say the African Republic has received pledges of aid from Taiwan totalling US$30 million over the next decade after deciding to formalise ties with Taipei.
Beijing also has been an active provider of aid, currently building Sao Tome's first national sports stadium along with residential and engineering projects.
China announced on Monday it was halting development projects in Sao Tome until the small state made clear whether it intended to establish ties with Taiwan.
China's Foreign Ministry said when news of the ties first broke that Sao Tome's move was "a short-sighted action that breaches trust and abandons justice".
China has regarded Taiwan as a rebel-held province not entitled to diplomatic recognition since the two split after a civil war in 1949.
Under China's ever-tightening diplomatic noose, Taipei is recognised by only 30 states, most of them small, poor and heavily dependent on Taipei's financial largesse.
Taipei brusquely severed ties with the Bahamas in May after learning the Caribbean nation was preparing to secure links with Beijing.
South Africa, Taiwan's biggest ally, said it would switch recognition to Beijing by the end of 1997.
